title: Economic effects of cormorant predation on catfish farms in the US Black Belt region (West Alabama and East Mississippi)
content:
Abstract

Losses to avian predators and the ensuing negative economic effects on US catfish farms have been well studied in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley. This study is the first to estimate the economic effects of predation by double-crested cormorants (Nannopterum auritum) on catfish farms in the Black Belt region (West Alabama and East Mississippi; named for its characteristic black prairie soils) of the Mississippi Flyway. Field data obtained from aerial surveys, observer counts, bird collections, and bioenergetic models were used to estimate economic effects on 32 catfish farming scenarios that modeled three farm sizes (32-ha, 124-ha, 592-ha), two species (channel or hybrid catfish), two aeration intensities (intensive or non-intensive), multiple or single-batch production, and two stocking densities (15 K or 20 K/ha). Lost farm revenue from cormorant predation averaged $4.9 million/year (range: $1.3 to $10.8 million/year), with an average economic output loss impact of $9.2 million/year (range of $2.5 to $20.0 million/year) to the Black Belt region. Profitability of Black Belt region catfish farms would be 31%–883% greater (depending on the farm/management scenario and intensity of predation in any given year) without losses to birds and without costs of bird deterrence. The combined economic effects of lost revenue from catfish consumed by cormorants and the increased on-farm costs of attempting to deter birds have likely contributed to the loss of catfish farms in this region in recent years. The recent availability of federal assistance to catfish farms that provides partial compensation for losses to avian predators, similar to that available to cattle farms, may increase retention of catfish farms and their contributions to the economy of the Black Belt region.
